item.title: Kazakhstan’s Nvidia Plans Put U.S. Export Rules in Focus as Astana Welcomes Sberbank and Yandex
item.description: Kazakhstan is welcoming Russian tech firms Sberbank and Yandex as Freedom Holding plans a $2 billion AI hub powered by Nvidia chips. Traders and consumers could gain affordable digital tools and ...
item.content:encoded:
Kazakhstan’s Nvidia Plans Put U.S. Export Rules in Focus as Astana Welcomes Sberbank and Yandex Kazakhstan is welcoming Russian tech firms Sberbank and Yandex as Freedom Holding plans a $2 billion AI hub powered by Nvidia chips. Traders and consumers could gain affordable digital tools and better Kazakh-language services, while policymakers face decisions on power supply, data protection and compliance with U.S. export controls. Devdiscourse News Desk | Updated: 28-11-2026 09:07 IST | Created: 28-11-2026 09:07 IST

Representative Image.

Country:

Kazakhstan

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Kazakhstan is courting Russian technology companies while laying the groundwork for an AI industry powered by American chips. On November 26, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow that Kazakhstan supported the work of Sberbank and Yandex in its market. A month earlier, Tokayev met Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang in Astana, and financial services group Freedom Holding outlined plans for a roughly $2 billion AI hub. For Kazakh traders and consumers, the payoff depends on whether that investment produces affordable services. For policymakers, it raises questions about who can use the computing capacity and on what terms.

Can small traders afford to use the new computing power? Freedom plans to open its first cluster of graphics processing units to cloud customers in 2027. Chief Executive Timur Turlov said the company was placing an order for an initial cluster of up to 300 servers powered by Nvidia's B300 chips. Freedom's annual filing describes the roughly $2 billion investment estimate as preliminary and subject to the project's final design. The public announcement gives a target year for cloud access, while the timing of server deliveries and customer pricing remain unclear.

Most traders would encounter the technology through software. A wholesaler could use an inventory tool to spot which goods are selling faster than expected. An online merchant could use a service that translates listings or answers routine customer questions in Kazakh and Russian. Renting computing time could lower the upfront cost for local software companies that build those tools. Whether merchants can afford the resulting products will depend on cloud prices, competition among providers and how much capacity smaller developers can book. Freedom says prospective customers have already expressed interest in leasing capacity for five years, making allocation an early issue to watch.

Consumers could gain better services, with new questions about their data For consumers, one practical gain would be better support in the language they use. A shopper could ask about a missing order or return in Kazakh and get a useful answer without switching languages. The value of that service depends on how well it handles everyday speech and whether it can pass a complicated case to someone who can resolve it. Lower operating costs could also help merchants offer better service, though any savings for shoppers would depend on how businesses price their products.

The risks become more consequential when AI handles bank records, purchase histories or government applications. Kazakhstan enacted an AI law in November 2025. As businesses adopt these tools, consumers will have a direct interest in who can see their records, whether information entered into a chatbot can be reused, and how to challenge an error that affects a payment or access to a service. Those outcomes depend on how the tools are deployed and how existing protections are enforced.

Moscow's chip constraints sharpen Astana's policy choices At the Moscow conference, Sberbank showcased updated AI models, while Putin identified electricity, grid capacity and access to sophisticated components as bottlenecks. U.S. export controls imposed after Russia's invasion of Ukraine restrict the supply of advanced technology to Russia. Reuters also reported that a Russian decree permits companies to use overseas data centres with approval from Russian security services. Sberbank and Yandex had made no public announcement about moving services abroad under that policy at the time of the conference.

Tokayev's remarks welcomed Russian businesses in Kazakhstan. Access to the planned Nvidia-powered hub would be a separate commercial and regulatory decision. Any such proposal would require a review of the applicable rules, the parties involved and the proposed use. For Kazakhstan, the stakes extend beyond a single contract. Domestic developers and investors planning around imported hardware need predictable access to it, and foreign suppliers need clarity about who will use it.

The 2027 launch will test power supply and access Freedom envisages a site with 100 megawatts of available power. That figure describes the planned site's power availability. The implications for the grid will depend on actual demand, where the electricity comes from and who pays for any network upgrades. For policymakers weighing further data-centre investment, those details will help establish what the project costs electricity users and what it delivers to domestic businesses.

The next milestones are confirmed server deliveries, a firm opening date, published prices and the terms on which smaller customers can rent computing time. Any agreements with Sberbank or Yandex will also warrant scrutiny for what they cover, from software sales to research or infrastructure. For traders and consumers, the clearest measure of progress will be whether Kazakh companies can afford to build services that people use in everyday commerce.

item.title: Russian scientists to search for ice up to 1.5 million years old in Antarctica

item.content:encoded:
Russian scientists to search for ice up to 1.5 million years old in Antarctica Staff from the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI) will set out in search of ancient ice dating back around 1.5 million years. Using this ice, polar researchers will study the concentration of greenhouse gases in the ancient atmosphere. This is important for verifying modern climate models, according to the website of the Russian Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment. ANI | Updated: 27-11-2026 21:50 IST | Created: 27-11-2026 21:50 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Russia

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Staff from the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI) will set out in search of ancient ice dating back around 1.5 million years. Using this ice, polar researchers will study the concentration of greenhouse gases in the ancient atmosphere. This is important for verifying modern climate models, according to the website of the Russian Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment. The composition of ice deposits holds information about past air temperatures. According to AARI Director Aleksander Makarov, around 50 million years ago, the concentration of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the Earth’s atmosphere was significantly higher than it is today. There was no ice sheet in Antarctica at that time, and sea levels were approximately 65 metres higher than they are now. The research aims to uncover crucial information about a major transition in Earth's climate history, when the periodicity of glacial cycles underwent significant changes. Scientists believe that examining ice samples from this period could help explain the factors behind these climatic shifts and improve the accuracy of climate predictions. "Our task is to find ice in Antarctica that is up to 1.5 million years old. It is at this juncture in the planet’s climate history that significant changes in the periodicity of glacial cycles are recorded. Understanding the reasons behind this transition is critically important for testing climate models. We need to understand where the boundaries of a climate suitable for life lie," Makarov said. Russia's Minister of Natural Resources and Environment Aleksander Kozlov said that findings from ancient Antarctic ice would expand the global scientific community's understanding of how Earth's climate developed over millions of years. He added that the research would also help scientists identify the natural limits of climate variability. Ice cores preserve traces of the atmosphere from the period in which they formed, allowing researchers to examine historical greenhouse gas concentrations and reconstruct past environmental conditions. Such findings can provide valuable evidence for understanding long-term climate patterns and assessing present-day climate changes. The search for ice dating back up to 1.5 million years is part of a long-term scientific programme. Russian researchers have already collected and analysed ancient ice samples estimated to be around 1.2 million years old. The upcoming expedition will seek to extend this research further into Earth's climate past. (ANI)

item.title: US goods trade deficit widens 10.7% to USD 149.5 billion in October as imports surge
item.description: The United States' goods trade deficit widened by 10.7 per cent month-on-month to USD 149.5 billion in October 2026, compared to USD 135.1 billion in September, as growth in imports outpaced that of ...
item.content:encoded:
US goods trade deficit widens 10.7% to USD 149.5 billion in October as imports surge The United States' goods trade deficit widened by 10.7 per cent month-on-month to USD 149.5 billion in October 2026, compared to USD 135.1 billion in September, as growth in imports outpaced that of exports, according to advance estimates released by the US Census Bureau on Friday. ANI | Updated: 27-11-2026 19:23 IST | Created: 27-11-2026 19:23 IST

Representative image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The United States' goods trade deficit widened by 10.7 per cent month-on-month to USD 149.5 billion in October 2026, compared to USD 135.1 billion in September, as growth in imports outpaced that of exports, according to advance estimates released by the US Census Bureau on Friday. On a year-on-year basis, the goods trade deficit surged by over 143 per cent from USD 61.4 billion recorded in October 2025. "The international trade deficit was $149.5 billion in October, up $14.4 billion from $135.1 billion in September," the US Census Bureau said in its Advance Economic Indicators Report. Goods imports rose by 6.1 per cent month-on-month to USD 365.3 billion in October, while exports increased by 3.2 per cent to USD 215.8 billion. "Exports of goods for October were $215.8 billion, $6.7 billion more than September exports. Imports of goods for October were $365.3 billion, $21.1 billion more than September imports," the report said. On an annual basis, US goods imports surged by 42.4 per cent, significantly outpacing the 10.6 per cent growth in exports. The sharp increase in imports was led by capital goods, which registered an 80 per cent year-on-year growth and an 8.5 per cent sequential increase to USD 171.4 billion in October. Imports of industrial supplies, including petroleum and petroleum products, increased by 33.5 per cent year-on-year, while consumer goods and automotive vehicle imports rose by 16.6 per cent and 8.4 per cent, respectively. On the exports front, capital goods recorded a 29.2 per cent year-on-year increase, while exports of industrial supplies rose by 3.6 per cent. However, exports of automotive vehicles and consumer goods declined by 5 per cent each. The widening of the goods trade deficit comes amid Washington's renewed push for tariffs on its trading partners over alleged structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. On November 25, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) announced proposed tariff actions following 14 investigations under Section 301 of US trade law. Washington has proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods, with certain exemptions, while indicating that the rate could be lowered to 17 per cent if India reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade addressing the findings of the investigation. Meanwhile, US wholesale inventories increased by 0.9 per cent month-on-month and 8.5 per cent year-on-year to USD 1,023.4 billion in October. Retail inventories also rose by 0.8 per cent sequentially and 5.1 per cent annually to USD 893.2 billion during the month. The figures are adjusted for seasonal variations but not for price changes. The October trade figures are advance estimates, with complete data to be published in the upcoming US International Trade in Goods and Services report. (ANI)
